     6→/**
     7→ * Hexi provides string adaptors that allow for control over how std::string and
     8→ * std::string_views are serialised. This is to ensure the element of least surprise
     9→ * in the case of handling strings that contain embedded null bytes.
    10→ * 
    11→ * raw: serialise the string exactly as-is
    12→ * 
    13→ * null_terminated: ensure the string is null-terminated. Strings with null bytes
    14→ * will trigger an assert in debug builds. This is to ensure that the input of
    15→ * a null_terminated serialisation exactly matches the output.
    16→ * 
    17→ * prefixed: writes the length of the string before the string's data. These strings
    18→ * can contain embedded null bytes.
    19→ * 
    20→ * prefixed_varint: writes the length of the string before the string's data with a compact
    21→ * varint coding. This is slower than prefixed but more compact.
    22→ * These strings can contain embedded null bytes.
    23→ * 
    24→ * const char* strings will always be written as null terminated strings and should be
    25→ * retrieved as such.
    26→ * 
    27→ * If no adaptor is provided, prefixed will be implicitly used. This is to ensure that
    28→ * the output will always match the input even in cases of embedded nulls.
    29→ */
    30→int main() {
    31→	std::string str { "The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog"};
    32→
    33→	// create stream
    34→	std::vector<char> buffer;
    35→	hexi::buffer_adaptor adaptor(buffer);
    36→	hexi::binary_stream stream(adaptor);
    37→
    38→	// serialise our string - will be prefixed by default
    39→	stream << str;
    40→
    41→	// serialise our string with null_terminated, will always be null terminated
    42→	stream << hexi::null_terminated(str);
    43→
    44→	// serialise our string by length prefixing
    45→	stream << hexi::prefixed(str);
    46→
    47→	// serialise our string by prefixing with a length varint
    48→	stream << hexi::prefixed_varint(str);
    49→
    50→	// serialise our string with raw, will not be terminated
    51→	stream << hexi::raw(str);
    52→
    53→	// read our strings back
    54→	std::string_view view;
    55→	stream >> view;
    56→	stream >> hexi::null_terminated(view);
    57→	stream >> hexi::prefixed(view);
    58→	stream >> hexi::prefixed_varint(view);
    59→
    60→	// retrieving a raw string is more complex - we need to know the size
    61→	// alternatively, we can write a terminating/sentinel byte manually and
    62→	// call find_first_of to determine length or to get a string_view with
    63→	// a call to stream.view();
    64→	std::string output;
    65→	output.resize(output.size());
    66→	stream.get(output.data(), output.size());
    67→}

1→#include <hexi.h>
     2→#include <string>
     3→#include <string_view>
     4→#include <vector>
     5→
     6→/**
     7→ * Hexi provides string adaptors that allow for control over how std::string and
     8→ * std::string_views are serialised. This is to ensure the element of least surprise
     9→ * in the case of handling strings that contain embedded null bytes.
    10→ * 
    11→ * raw: serialise the string exactly as-is
    12→ * 
    13→ * null_terminated: ensure the string is null-terminated. Strings with null bytes
    14→ * will trigger an assert in debug builds. This is to ensure that the input of
    15→ * a null_terminated serialisation exactly matches the output.
    16→ * 
    17→ * prefixed: writes the length of the string before the string's data. These strings
    18→ * can contain embedded null bytes.
    19→ * 
    20→ * prefixed_varint: writes the length of the string before the string's data with a compact
    21→ * varint coding. This is slower than prefixed but more compact.
    22→ * These strings can contain embedded null bytes.
    23→ * 
    24→ * const char* strings will always be written as null terminated strings and should be
    25→ * retrieved as such.
    26→ * 
    27→ * If no adaptor is provided, prefixed will be implicitly used. This is to ensure that
    28→ * the output will always match the input even in cases of embedded nulls.
    29→ */
    30→int main() {
    31→	std::string str { "The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog"};
    32→
    33→	// create stream
    34→	std::vector<char> buffer;
    35→	hexi::buffer_adaptor adaptor(buffer);
    36→	hexi::binary_stream stream(adaptor);
    37→
    38→	// serialise our string - will be prefixed by default
    39→	stream << str;
    40→
    41→	// serialise our string with null_terminated, will always be null terminated
    42→	stream << hexi::null_terminated(str);
    43→
    44→	// serialise our string by length prefixing
    45→	stream << hexi::prefixed(str);
    46→
    47→	// serialise our string by prefixing with a length varint
    48→	stream << hexi::prefixed_varint(str);
    49→
    50→	// serialise our string with raw, will not be terminated
    51→	stream << hexi::raw(str);
    52→
    53→	// read our strings back
    54→	std::string_view view;
    55→	stream >> view;
    56→	stream >> hexi::null_terminated(view);
    57→	stream >> hexi::prefixed(view);
    58→	stream >> hexi::prefixed_varint(view);
    59→
    60→	// retrieving a raw string is more complex - we need to know the size
    61→	// alternatively, we can write a terminating/sentinel byte manually and
    62→	// call find_first_of to determine length or to get a string_view with
    63→	// a call to stream.view();
    64→	std::string output;
    65→	output.resize(output.size());
    66→	stream.get(output.data(), output.size());
    67→}

    16→// instance on the same thread shares the same underlying memory.
    17→// As a rule of thumb, an instance should never be touched by any thread
    18→// other than the one on which it was created, not even if synchronised
    19→// ... unless you're positive it won't result in the allocator being called.
    20→// 
    21→// Minimum memory usage is intrusive_storage<block_size> * count.
    22→// Additional blocks are not added if the original is exhausted ('colony' structure),
    23→// so the allocator will fall back to the system allocator instead.
    24→//
    25→// Pros: extremely fast allocation/deallocation for many instances per thread
    26→// Cons: everything else.

    33→	typename storage_type = std::byte>
    34→using dynamic_tls_buffer = dynamic_buffer<block_size, storage_type,
    35→	tls_block_allocator<typename dynamic_buffer<block_size>::storage_type, count, no_ref_counting, entrant_policy>
    36→>;

     6→/**
     7→ * Hexi provides string adaptors that allow for control over how std::string and
     8→ * std::string_views are serialised. This is to ensure the element of least surprise
     9→ * in the case of handling strings that contain embedded null bytes.
    10→ * 
    11→ * raw: serialise the string exactly as-is
    12→ * 
    13→ * null_terminated: ensure the string is null-terminated. Strings with null bytes
    14→ * will trigger an assert in debug builds. This is to ensure that the input of
    15→ * a null_terminated serialisation exactly matches the output.
    16→ * 
    17→ * prefixed: writes the length of the string before the string's data. These strings
    18→ * can contain embedded null bytes.
    19→ * 
    20→ * prefixed_varint: writes the length of the string before the string's data with a compact
    21→ * varint coding. This is slower than prefixed but more compact.
    22→ * These strings can contain embedded null bytes.
    23→ * 
    24→ * const char* strings will always be written as null terminated strings and should be
    25→ * retrieved as such.

     7→ * Hexi provides string adaptors that allow for control over how std::string and

    11→ * raw: serialise the string exactly as-is

    13→ * null_terminated: ensure the string is null-terminated. Strings with null bytes
    14→ * will trigger an assert in debug builds. This is to ensure that the input of
    15→ * a null_terminated serialisation exactly matches the output.
    16→ * 
    17→ * prefixed: writes the length of the string before the string's data. These strings
    18→ * can contain embedded null bytes.
    19→ * 
    20→ * prefixed_varint: writes the length of the string before the string's data with a compact
    21→ * varint coding. This is slower than prefixed but more compact.
    22→ * These strings can contain embedded null bytes.
    23→ * 
    24→ * const char* strings will always be written as null terminated strings and should be
    25→ * retrieved as such.
    26→ * 
    27→ * If no adaptor is provided, prefixed will be implicitly used. This is to ensure that
    28→ * the output will always match the input even in cases of embedded nulls.

13→ 14→Hexi is a lightweight, header-only C++23 library for safely handling binary data from arbitrary sources (but primarily network data). It sits somewhere between manually memcpying bytes from network buffers and full-blown serialisation libraries. 15→ 16→Some of the protocols Hexi is used to handle include [DNS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_Name_System), [STUN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STUN), [NAT Port Mapping Protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAT_Port_Mapping_Protocol), [Port Control Protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Control_Protocol), World of Warcraft (emulators) and GameSpy (emulators). Of course, nothing stops you from defining your own! 17→ 18→The design goals are ease of use, safety when dealing with untrusted data and in the face of programmer mistakes, a reasonable level of flexibility, and keeping overhead to a minimum. 19→ 20→What Hexi doesn't offer: versioning, conversion between different formats, handling of text-based formats, unloading the dishwasher. 21→ 22→Hexi is dual-licensed under MIT and Apache License, Version 2.0. This means you can use Hexi under the license you prefer. 23→ 24→ 25→ 26→Incorporating Hexi into your project is simple! The easiest way is to simply copy `hexi.h` from `single_include` into your own project. If you'd rather only include what you use, you can add `include` to your include paths or incorporate it into your own CMake project with `target_link_library`. To build the unit tests, run CMake with `ENABLE_TESTING`. 27→ 28→Here's what some libraries might call a very simple motivating example: 29→ 30→```cpp 31→#include 32→#include 33→#include 34→#include 35→ 36→struct LoginPacket { 37→ uint64_t user_id; 38→ uint64_t timestamp; 39→ std::array ipv6; 40→}; 41→ 42→auto deserialise(std::span network_buffer) { 43→ hexi::buffer_adaptor adaptor(network_buffer); // wrap the buffer 44→ hexi::binary_stream stream(adaptor); // create a binary stream 45→ 46→ // deserialise! 47→ LoginPacket packet; 48→ stream >> packet; 49→ return packet; 50→} 51→ 52→auto serialise(const LoginPacket& packet) { 53→ std::vector buffer; 54→ hexi::buffer_adaptor adaptor(buffer); // wrap the buffer 55→ hexi::binary_stream stream(adaptor); // create a binary stream 56→ 57→ // serialise! 58→ stream << packet; 59→ return buffer; 60→} 61→``` 62→By default, Hexi will try to serialise basic structures such as our `LoginPacket` if they meet requirements for being safe to directly copy the bytes. Now, for reasons of portability, it's not recommended that you do things this way unless you're positive that the data layout is identical on the system that wrote the data. Not to worry, this is easily solved. Plus, we didn't do any error or endianness handling. All in good time. 63→ 64→ 65→ 66→The two classes you'll primarily deal with are `buffer_adaptor` and `binary_stream`. 67→ 68→`binary_stream` takes a container as its argument and is used to do the reading and writing. It doesn't know much about the details of the underlying container. 69→ 70→To support containers that weren't written to be used with Hexi, `buffer_adaptor` is used as a wrapper that `binary_stream` can interface with. As with `binary_stream`, it also provides read and write operations but at a lower level. 71→ 72→`buffer_adaptor` can wrap any contiguous container or view that provides `data` and `size` member functions. From the standard library, that means the following can be used out of the box: 73→- [x] std::array 74→- [x] std::span 75→- [x] std::string_view 76→- [x] std::string 77→- [x] std::vector 78→ 79→Plenty of non-standard library containers will work out of the box, too, as long as they provide a vaguely similar API. 80→ 81→The container's value type must be a byte type (e.g. `char`, `std::byte`, `uint8_t`). `std::as_bytes` can be used as a workaround if this poses a problem. 82→ 83→ 84→ 85→Hexi supports custom containers, including non-contiguous containers. In fact, there's a non-contiguous container included in the library. You simply need to provide a few functions such as `read` and `size` to allow the `binary_stream` class to be able to use it. 86→ 87→`static_buffer.h` provides a simple example of a custom container that can be used directly with `binary_stream`. 88→ 89→ 90→ 91→As mentioned, Hexi is intended to be safe to use even when dealing with untrusted data. An example might be network messages that have been manipulated to try to trick your code into reading out of bounds. 92→ 93→`binary_stream` performs bounds checking to ensure that it will never read more data than the buffer has available and optionally allows you to specify an upper bound on the amount of data to read. This can be useful when you have multiple messages in a buffer and want to limit the deserialisation from potentially eating into the next. 94→ 95→```cpp 96→buffer_t buffer; 97→// ... read data 98→hexi::binary_stream stream(buffer, 32); // will never read more than 32 bytes 99→``` 100→ 101→ 102→ 103→The default error handling mechanism is exceptions. Upon encountering a problem with reading data, an exception derived from `hexi::exception` will be thrown. These are: 104→ 105→- `hexi::buffer_underrun` - attempt to read out of bounds 106→- `hexi::stream_read_limit` - attempt to read more than the imposed limit 107→ 108→Exceptions from `binary_stream` can be disabled by specifying `no_throw` as an argument. This argument eliminates exception branches at compile-time, so there's zero run-time overhead. 109→```cpp 110→hexi::binary_stream stream(buffer, hexi::no_throw); 111→``` 112→Regardless of the error handling mechanism you use, the state of a `binary_stream` can be checked as follows: 113→```cpp 114→hexi::binary_stream stream(buffer, hexi::no_throw); state != hexi::stream_state::ok) { 124→ // handle error 125→} 126→``` 127→ 128→ 129→ 130→In the first example, reading our `LoginPacket` would only work as expected if the program that wrote the data laid everything out in the same way as our own program. 131→This might not be the case for reasons of architecture differences, compiler flags, etc. 132→ 133→Here's the same example but doing it portably. 134→```cpp 135→#include 136→#include 137→#include 138→#include 139→#include 140→#include 141→ 142→// an example structure that has separate serialise and deserialise functions 143→struct LoginPacket { 144→ uint64_t user_id; 171→ } 172→ 173→ return stream; 174→ } 175→}; 176→ 177→// an example of a packet that can serialise and deserialise with the same function 178→struct LogoutPacket { 179→ std::string username; 180→ std::uint32_t user_id; 181→ std::uint8_t has_timestamp; 182→ std::uint64_t timestamp; // pretend this is optional & big endian in the protocol 183→ 184→ void serialise(auto& stream) const { 185→ stream(username, user_id); 186→ 187→ if (has_timestamp) { 188→ stream(hexi::endian::be(timestamp)); 189→ 190→ // can also do this to write a single field: 191→ // stream & hexi::endian::be(timestamp); 192→ } 193→ } 194→}; 195→ 196→ 197→// pretend we're reading network data 198→void read() { 199→ std::vector buffer; 200→ const auto bytes_read = socket.read(buffer); 201→ 202→ // ... logic for determining packet type, etc 203→ 204→ bool result {}; 205→ 206→ switch (packet_type) { 207→ case login_packet: 208→ result = handle_login_packet(buffer); 209→ break; 210→ case logout_packet: 211→ result = handle_logout_packet(buffer); 212→ break; 213→ } 214→ 215→ // ... handle result 216→} 217→ 218→auto handle_login_packet(std::span buffer) { 219→ hexi::buffer_adaptor adaptor(buffer); 220→ 221→ /** 222→ * hexi::endian::little tells the stream to convert to/from 223→ * little-endian unless told otherwise by using the endian 224→ * adaptors. If no argument is provided, it does not perform 225→ * any conversions by default. 226→ */ 227→ hexi::binary_stream stream(adaptor, hexi::endian::little); 228→ 229→ LoginPacket packet; 230→ stream >> packet; 231→ 232→ if (stream) { 233→ // ... do something with the packet 234→ return true; 235→ } else { 236→ return false; 237→ } 238→} 239→ 240→auto handle_logout_packet(std::span buffer) { 241→ hexi::buffer_adaptor adaptor(buffer); 242→ hexi::binary_stream stream(adaptor, hexi::endian::little); 243→ 244→ LogoutPacket packet; 245→ stream << packet; 246→ 247→ /** 248→ * alternative methods: 249→ * stream.serialise(packet); 250→ * 251→ * or: 252→ * 253→ * hexi::stream_read_adaptor adaptor(stream); 254→ * packet.serialise(adaptor); 255→ */ 256→ 257→ if (stream) { 258→ // ... do something with the packet 259→ return true; 260→ } else { 261→ return false; 262→ } 263→} 264→``` 265→ 266→This example is fully portable and is even independent of the platform byte order. By specifying the endianness of the stream, it'll automagically convert all endian-sensitive data to the requested byte order. 267→The default argument is `hexi::endian::native`, which will perform no conversions, while `hexi::endian::big` and `hexi::endian::little` will perform conversions if required. 268→ 269→If your protocol contains mixed endianness, you can use the endian adaptors to specify the desired byte order when streaming 270→the data, as shown in the above example. 271→ 272→Best of all, because this is handled by templates, there is zero runtime cost if no conversion is required 273→(i.e. the native byte order matches the requested byte order) and constant values can be converted 274→at compile-time. For example, specifying `hexi::endian::little` on a little-endian platform will generate zero 275→code. 276→ 277→`docs/examples/endian.cpp` provides examples for byte order handling functionality. 278→ 279→As for the serialisation functions, if you want the function bodies to be in a source file, it's recommended that you provide your own `using` alias for your `binary_stream` type. 280→The alternative is to use the polymorphic equivalents, `pmc::buffer_adaptor` and `pmc::binary_stream`, which allow you to change the underlying buffer type at runtime but at the potential cost of virtual call overhead (devirtualisation not withstanding) and lacking some functionality that doesn't mesh well with polymorphism. 281→ 282→How you structure your code is up to you, this is just one way of doing it. 283→ 284→ 285→ 286→Handling strings need a little thought. `std::string` and `std::string_view` are allowed to contain embedded nulls, even if it's rarely done. 287→ 288→To adhere to the principle of least surprise, Hexi defaults to reading & writing these types with a length prefix. This ensures that writing 289→such a string and reading it back will give you the correct result regardless of the contents. 290→ 291→In the majority of cases, you'll want to read/write strings as null-terminated. To do this, use a string adaptor, as such: 292→ 293→```cpp 294→hexi::binary_stream stream(...); 295→std::string foo { "No surprises here!" }; 296→ 297→// write it 298→stream << hexi::null_terminated(foo); 299→ 300→// read it back 301→stream >> hexi::null_terminated(foo); 302→``` 303→ 304→This is not the default because writing strings that may contain embedded null bytes would result in a truncated string on reading back. Read them back with the `null_terminated` adaptor. 307→ 308→Other adaptors, such as `prefixed_varint`, are available. See `docs/examples/string_handling.cpp` for usage examples. 309→ 310→ 311→ 312→Here's a very quick rundown on some of the included extras. 313→- `hexi::file_buffer` 314→ - For dealing with binary files. Simples. 315→- `hexi::static_buffer` 316→ - Fixed-size networking buffer for when you know the upper bound on the amount of data you'll need to send or receive in one go. Essentially a wrapper around `std::array` but with added state tracking. Handy if you need to deserialise in multiple steps (read packet header, dispatch, read packet body). 317→- `hexi::dynamic_buffer` 318→ - Resizeable buffer for when you want to deal with occasional large reads/writes without having to allocate the space up front. Internally, it adds additional allocations to accommodate extra data rather than requesting a larger allocation and copying data as `std::vector` would. It reuses allocated blocks where possible and has support for Asio (Boost or standalone). Effectively, it's a linked list buffer. 319→- `hexi::tls_block_allocator` 320→ - Allows many instances of `dynamic_buffer` to share a larger pool of pre-allocated memory, with each thread having its own pool. Running serialisation twice might sound 326→ inefficient, but compilers can often calculate the end result of serialising to `null_buffer` at compile-time, or distill 327→ it down to a few instructions of arithmetic. 328→ 329→ 330→ 331→We're at the end of the overview, but there's more to discover if you decide to give Hexi a shot.
